spans.t: This is a small book for fourteen slow days. It is made to go with the Camino del Norte, the road that runs from Irun to Santiago de Compostela, ~820 km. You read one day at a time, whether you are walking or at home.

The road is far longer than the book. If you read one day for each walking day, the book will run out early, and you can read it again. To make it last, read a day every second or third day, or keep one for a rest day.
Why this poem for this road
Dante's
Purgatorio

is the story of a climb. A poet and his guide come out of the dark onto a shore at dawn and begin to walk up a mountain, one stage at a time: a gate, seven ledges that wind round the slope, and a garden at the top. Each ledge has its own weight to put down, and the way is steep at first and kinder higher up. The poem begins by the sea.

The Norte is a long road of sea and hills, and it too is taken in stages. The poem notices what any walker will know: the first hard hill, the hour when the heart turns for home, a row of people leaning on each other, a night when you cannot go on, a guide who has done all he can.
A day, in two parts
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from the poem, in the exact words of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's translation. It is old-fashioned English (
thou
doth
o'er

), which slows the eye. Read it twice, the second time aloud if you can. Where a stretch is skipped inside a passage, a mark like this shows it: …. Longfellow wrote in lines of verse, grouped in threes; here the lines are joined with a space, so the breaks are not shown.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Dante's. It starts from something on the road and lets the passage open it. It says what the passage says, where it is hard, and what it might ask of an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention. Please read on a bench or in a café, not while you walk along a road.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back at the day you have lived, and two or three gentle questions. Nothing needs writing down.
A short prayer.
Original and short, and not Dante's. If you pray, pray it. If you pray differently, change the words. If you do not pray, say it as a wish.

spans.t: A poem of its time, and who it is for
The
Purgatorio
is the middle part of the
Divine Comedy

, written in the early fourteenth century. It belongs to the medieval Catholic imagination: its mountain is the poem's picture of purgatory, as that faith described it, and its people pray, sing hymns and speak as believers. We say so plainly so that nobody is surprised. We do not explain that belief or argue for it. We read the mountain as a picture of a climb, and its people as walkers with something to put down.

People walk the Camino for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All of them are welcome here. You do not need to share the poet's faith to know what he noticed about tiredness, comparison, anger and the wish to go on. You do not need to have read the poem's first part. Where a name from Dante's own day matters, we explain it in a clause.
The shape of the fourteen days
The days follow the climb, in the order of the poem.

items.t: Days 1 to 3, the shore and the foot of the mountain.
Setting out, the hard beginning, and the hour of the evening bell.
Day 4, the gate.
A threshold, three steps and a warning not to look back.
Days 5 to 11, the ledges.
Pride (two days), envy, anger, sloth, greed and appetite, one after another.
Days 12 to 14, the top.
A wall of fire to cross and a night on the stairs, a guide who lets go, and the last waters, where the climb ends.

spans.t: The shape is a guide, not a timetable. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer and leave the rest for the morning.
One phrase you will meet:
Buen Camino
, which walkers say to one another on the road, roughly, may your Way go well.
Read slowly. The poem was meant to be heard, one line at a time.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The poet

Dante Alighieri was born in Florence in 1265 and died in 1321. He was a poet, and he also took part in the public life of his city. In 1302 Florence sent him into exile, and he did not go home again. He wrote his great poem during those years of exile, over roughly the last dozen or so years of his life. The file we quote from gives only his name, so these few facts are general knowledge. We say "roughly" where a figure is not exact, and we have not tried to say more than we know.
The poem
The poem's own title was simply the
Comedy
; later readers added
Divine
. It has three parts: the
Inferno
, the
Purgatorio
and the
Paradiso
. In each, the poet is the traveller, so the "I" in the passages is Dante's. In the first two he has a guide, the Roman poet Virgil, who also wrote the
Aeneid
. In the Italian, each of the three parts ends on the same word,
stelle
, which means stars. The
Purgatorio
does, as you will see on the last day.

This book uses only the middle part. It has thirty-three cantos, which is what the poem calls its chapters, and it begins just after the first part ends: the poet and his guide have come up out of the dark onto a shore, and in front of them stands a mountain. From the shore and the foot of the slope, they climb to a gate, then up seven ledges round the mountain, then to a garden at the top. The poem says they can climb only by day. You do not need to have read the first part. Everything you need is said in the day you are reading.

The poem belongs to the medieval Catholic imagination, and the mountain is its picture of purgatory, a place where souls headed for heaven are made ready. That belief is the poem's own, and we neither explain it nor argue for it. We read the poem as a pilgrim's climb, and we keep to what it shows.
Why it suits a pilgrim

It is a poem about walking. It has stages and a guide, a hard first stretch and a kinder one later, a night when no one can go on, and a goal that is a long way off and then, quite suddenly, is not. It keeps comparing itself to pilgrims: the word
pilgrim

turns up in five places in this translation, and every one of the five is in a passage in this book. The poet also admits, in his own voice, that he is tired, afraid and slow to understand, which is good company for a long road.

It is a hard poem too, and a poem of the fourteenth century. It is full of Dante's neighbours and enemies, and in places it is severe about what people have done. The politics we have left out. Some of the punishments are strange, and where a passage is strange we say so, and leave you to make up your own mind. We chose the passages that speak most plainly to someone on a road.
The translation, the edition and the licence

The English in the passages is by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, the American poet, who died in 1882. His translation of the whole poem was published in 1867; that date is general knowledge, since the file does not state a year. He wrote in unrhymed English lines, in groups of three. Because he died long ago, the translation is in the public domain. It is available from Project Gutenberg as ebook number 1002, under the title
Divine Comedy, Longfellow's Translation, Purgatory
, and every quotation in this book was checked against that text, word for word.
The file begins with a list of contents with a short summary of each canto. We have not used any of it. We quote only the poem itself, and none of the file's other matter.

What we changed in the passages is nothing, with three small exceptions. The lines of verse are joined with a space, so the line breaks are not shown. Where we skip a stretch inside a passage, a mark like this shows it: …. And where a speech goes on past the edge of our passage, we cut at a full stop and leave out any quotation mark that opens or closes beyond it, so that none is left hanging. The old spellings and endings are kept as they are. The fourteen passages come from sixteen of the thirty-three cantos. The choice of the passages and their order, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours, and they are original.
Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.
What changes in your eyes when the long dark is behind you and the road is in front?
The passage

paras.t: To run o’er better waters hoists its sail The little vessel of my genius now, That leaves behind itself a sea so cruel; … Sweet colour of the oriental sapphire, That was upgathered in the cloudless aspect Of the pure air, as far as the first circle, Unto mine eyes did recommence delight Soon as I issued forth from the dead air, Which had with sadness filled mine eyes and breast. … The dawn was vanquishing the matin hour Which fled before it, so that from afar I recognised the trembling of the sea. Along the solitary plain we went As one who unto the lost road returns, And till he finds it seems to go in vain. … There he begirt me as the other pleased; O marvellous! for even as he culled The humble plant, such it sprang up again Suddenly there where he uprooted it.

spans.t: Reflection

Before the sun is up, a coast has almost no colour. The sea is a grey sheet, the sky is a paler one, and the road is a line between them that you follow by feel. Then, in the space of a few minutes, something is added. Blue comes first, or a thin pink along the edge of the water, and the sheet turns into the sea. If you are walking when it happens, you may find you have stopped without deciding to.

That is the moment this poem begins with. Dante has just climbed out of Hell, and the first thing he tells us is a colour. It is the deep blue of an eastern sapphire, spread through the clear air as far as the rim of the sky, and with it, he says, delight begins again in his eyes, after the dead air
Which had with sadness filled mine eyes and breast
. He is a long way from any summit. He has only come up onto a beach at daybreak. But the poem treats that as the whole gift of the first morning: to see again.

He does something with the poem itself, too. He says his little vessel now hoists its sail to run over better waters, and leaves behind a sea so cruel. The cruel sea is the first part of the poem. This part is a voyage upward, and it starts from a real shore in real light.

At the water's edge someone is waiting: an old man alone, with a long beard streaked with white and a face so lit by four stars that he seems to have the sun in front of him. He challenges the two strangers. Who are they, and who has led them out of the eternal prison? Virgil, the guide, makes the younger man bow with his hand and his words, and answers for them both. This one, he says, is looking for liberty,
which is so dear
, as the old man knows, because he gave up his life for it at Utica. Readers know him as Cato.

Then the old man hands out the first work of the climb, and it is small. Go, he says, and gird this one about with a smooth rush, and wash his face, so that every stain is cleaned away. An eye clouded by any mist should not go before the first angel. Rushes grow along the foot of the island, where the waves strike. No other plant that puts out leaf or hardens can live there, he says, because it does not give way to the shocks. Where the water hits, only the plant that bends survives.
So the climb begins with a wash and a belt of reed. Not armour, and not a plan. The passage ends on the quietest detail of all: Dante picks the humble plant, and it grows again
Suddenly there where he uprooted it

What would it ask of you to begin like that? Most beginnings carry some show: the new boots, the early start, the story you will tell about starting. The poem begins with a washed face and a stalk of something that bends. You might take the hint at six in the morning. Wash, if there is water to hand. And let your first plan be a reed rather than a wall, something that gives when the road pushes and is still standing when the road is done.

Two things are worth saying plainly. The first is that Dante's dawn is a gift. He has not earned that sapphire; he has been brought here. Not every first morning will look like it, and the poem does not pretend so. Straight after the blue come a stern old man and a long empty plain. Look at the third stretch of our passage, where he and his guide go along the solitary plain
As one who unto the lost road returns, And till he finds it seems to go in vain

. That may be the more honest picture of the first days. You are on the right road and cannot yet tell, and until something confirms it, the walking feels like wandering. If that is your morning, you are not failing the poem. It has a line for you.

The second is smaller. Nothing here promises that the second morning will be like the first, and the poem does not promise it either. It promises only what is in the passage: a first light, a face to wash, and a plant that grows back. That is enough to start on.
For the walk

items.t: What is the first thing I can see clearly this morning?

Somewhere in the first hour, stop and wash your face if there is water to hand, a tap, a fountain or your bottle. If there is not, wipe it with your hand and breathe. Then say aloud, if nobody is near, the colour of the sky or the sea. That is all. Let that colour be your whole reading for a minute, and carry the question for the hour.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The sapphire is a long way back now. Whatever colour the sky had this morning, the day has used it up, and you are sitting somewhere with your shoes off, most likely, and your feet making their first report.

Let the day come back in the order it happened. The start: did you wash, or stop, or look about you? Or was it a scramble of straps and zips and a worry about the time? Neither is a failure. It is only worth knowing how you began.

Then think of the middle of the day, the stretch the poem calls the solitary plain. Most days have one: a long straight, a road beside traffic, an hour when nothing happens and you quietly doubt that you are in the right place. Was there such an hour today, and what did you do with it? You may simply have walked on, and that counts. The man in the poem does no more. He goes on, and it only seems in vain until he finds the road.

After that, the reed. Something had to bend today. A plan changed, a stage ended sooner or later than you meant, someone walked faster or slower than you, a bed was not the bed you hoped for. The small things are the ones we resist hardest. Did you give way, or stiffen? There is no right answer tonight. It is enough to know which you did. If you gave way even once, however small, that was the plant doing what it is for.

A word about the first evening of a long road. It is often the strangest. Nothing is where it should be, and you are tired in places you did not know you had. It is easy to read that as a verdict, that you are not up to it or have made a mistake. More likely it is only a first evening, and the body is reporting on a job it has not done before. Give it a night before you judge it. If your feet are sore, see to them before anything else, and if anything worries you beyond ordinary soreness, ask a pharmacist or a doctor.

The washing is worth repeating tonight. It was the first task the old man set, and it takes half a minute: face, hands, the back of the neck. Let the dust of the road go with the water. Whatever is not dust will still be there in the morning, and you can meet it then, rested. It is a way of closing the day as the poem opened it.

And if the sky is clear and it is safe to step outside, look up for a minute before bed. You do not need to know the name of a single star. The poem will end on that word, and it is a good one to fall asleep under.

items.t: What did I see clearly today that I would have missed in a hurry?
When did the road feel like wandering, and what did I do then?
What had to bend today, and did I let it?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the light that came back this morning. Wash from my face and my mind whatever I do not need to carry. Teach me to bend where I would break. Let me sleep tonight, and begin again tomorrow.
What if the climb is hardest now, and kinder later?
The passage

paras.t: Spent with fatigue was I, when I began: “O my sweet Father! turn thee and behold How I remain alone, unless thou stay!” “O son,” he said, “up yonder drag thyself,” Pointing me to a terrace somewhat higher, Which on that side encircles all the hill. These words of his so spurred me on, that I Strained every nerve, behind him scrambling up, Until the circle was beneath my feet. Thereon ourselves we seated both of us Turned to the East, from which we had ascended, For all men are delighted to look back. … And he to me: “This mount is such, that ever At the beginning down below ’tis tiresome, And aye the more one climbs, the less it hurts. Therefore, when it shall seem so pleasant to thee, That going up shall be to thee as easy As going down the current in a boat, Then at this pathway’s ending thou wilt be; There to repose thy panting breath expect; No more I answer; and this I know for true.” … And as he finished uttering these words, A voice close by us sounded: “Peradventure Thou wilt have need of sitting down ere that.”

spans.t: Reflection

There is a particular hill on the first days of a long walk. It is not the steepest you will meet. But the legs have not yet learned the work, the pack has not found its place on your back, and the top is out of sight behind a bend. You can stand at the bottom and feel the whole road piled up in that one slope.
Dante is at that point. The passage opens with him
Spent with fatigue

, and he does what tired people do: he asks his guide to stop, because otherwise he will be left behind and alone. Virgil does not make a speech. He points to a ledge a little higher up, the one that circles the whole hill, and tells him to drag himself up as far as that. The words spur Dante so hard that he strains every nerve and scrambles after him until the ledge is under his feet.
The guide's move is neat. He does not offer the summit, which is out of sight and would be crushing. He offers the next ledge, which is near enough to reach.
Then they sit, facing east, back the way they came. The poem gives its reason in a short line:
For all men are delighted to look back.

Walkers know this at once. You reach a bend and turn, and there is the place you slept, small and level and already part of a story. It is one of the few free pleasures of a climb, and Virgil, who hates to waste time, allows it.

Dante then asks what every tired person asks: how far is it? And Virgil gives the best-known promise in the poem. The mountain is made so, he says, that at the beginning, down below, it is tiring, and the more one climbs, the less it hurts. When going up feels as easy as going down a river in a boat, you will be at the end of this path, and there you can rest your panting breath. Then, a little drily: no more answer, but he knows it to be true.

Virgil gives no distance. He gives a rule and a sign. You will know it by how it feels, and that is all he says. It is an honest kind of encouragement. It does not say that the end is near. It says that the effort changes.
Dante is not left to enjoy it in peace. A voice close by says,
Peradventure Thou wilt have need of sitting down ere that.

You will probably want to sit before then. It comes from behind a great rock they had not noticed, where some people stand in the shade as if through idleness. One of them, who looks worn out, is sitting with his arms round his knees and his face down between them. Dante knows him, and calls him Belacqua, and a little laughter comes to his lips at the slumped figure. He asks whether the man is waiting for an escort or has fallen back into his old habit. The answer is a question that the whole poem has to face:
O brother, what's the use of climbing?

Two things stand side by side here, and the poem lets both stand. The mountain gets easier, and a man who has settled into the shade has a point, because climbing is hard and nobody is making him. Virgil does not sneer at him, and he does not stay. Dante bends near and speaks with something like affection, and then goes on. Resting is not the fault. The two travellers have just sat down themselves. What the poem notices in the figure behind the rock is the settling: knees drawn up, face hidden, a question that has quietly become an answer.

What does this ask of an ordinary day? Three small things. Choose the nearer ledge. When the top is out of sight, pick the next bend, the next tree, the next waymark, and let that be the whole task. Turn round at the top of it and look back. And sit down on purpose, for a few minutes, so that you are not caught by a rock and a stranger's voice.

We cannot promise the road will ease. Hills do not read poetry, and a road of hills does not promise to flatten. What the poem claims is about the climber. You may find that the first hill is the one that feels like the whole road, and that a hill in the second week is one you almost forget. That is a hope, not a rule, and the body keeps its own timetable. A sore body is also not the same as an injured one. Pain that sharpens, swells or does not ease is a matter for a pharmacist or a doctor, not for poetry. In an emergency, call 112.
For the walk

items.t: Which ledge, rather than the summit, is my next one?

When the top is out of sight, choose something near, a bend, a tree, a waymark, and walk to it as if it were the whole task. When you reach it, turn round and look back for three breaths before going on. Do this three times in the next hour. If you need to sit down, sit on purpose and give it a count of a hundred, then stand.

spans.t: At the end of the day
The second evening has its own character. The novelty of the first has worn off, and the stiffness that was waiting for you has arrived. Nothing is wrong. It is only the hill, now in the body.

Tonight you can do what the two travellers did on their ledge: sit and look back. Try it in the mind. Start from where you are, and run the day backwards, bed first, then the last stretch, then the middle, then the early morning, as if you had turned round at the top of a slope. Pick out three places. They need not be beautiful. A bar, a field edge, a bend in a lane will do. Notice how small the morning looks from here, and how much of it is already behind you. If you have a map or a list of the stages, run a finger along the stretch you walked today and then along tomorrow's. The first is solid, drawn by your own legs. The second is only a line. It is a quiet pleasure to watch the ground turn from one into the other.

Then think about the hills. There was probably one that looked like the whole road while you stood below it. How did it go? Did you give yourself a nearer goal, or keep your eyes on the top? And was there a moment like the one behind the rock, a point when you wanted to stay where you were and let the day go on without you? Be fair to it. A rest is a good thing, and the poem does not mock it. Tonight is a good time to tell which kind you took. The kind you take is short and has a reason, and afterwards you stand up. The kind that takes you lasts longer than you meant and has no reason except that standing up is hard. Neither is a sin. Only the second is worth knowing about.
If today was easier than yesterday, be glad of it without making it a promise for tomorrow. If it was harder, that is not a bad sign. Bodies adapt at their own speed, and nobody can set it for them.
There is one more thing to do with the question from behind the rock,
what's the use of climbing?

Tonight it may sound less like Belacqua's voice and more like your own. Give it an honest answer, in a sentence, for nobody but yourself. You may not have a reason yet. That is allowed, and a reason can arrive after the start. If you do have one, say it once, quietly, and let it be among the last things you think of before you sleep. If you do not, let the question stay open. It will keep until morning, and it is not a verdict on the day.
So let the legs be heavy on the mattress. Heavy legs are what the day was for. Drink some water, eat something, and let sleep be the last ledge of the day.

items.t: Which near ledge got me through today, when the top was out of sight?
When I turned and looked back, what did I see?
Was my rest today a pause or a settling, and how can I tell?

spans.t: A short prayer
Be near me on the steep part. Give me a ledge I can reach, and the sense to sit when I should. Let my legs be heavy and my sleep be deep. In the morning, let me stand up without being asked twice.

chapters.title: Day 3. The hour of the bell

spans.t: What does the evening do to a heart that has left home?
The passage

paras.t: ’Twas now the hour that turneth back desire In those who sail the sea, and melts the heart, The day they’ve said to their sweet friends farewell, And the new pilgrim penetrates with love, If he doth hear from far away a bell That seemeth to deplore the dying day, When I began to make of no avail My hearing, and to watch one of the souls Uprisen, that begged attention with its hand. It joined and lifted upward both its palms, Fixing its eyes upon the orient, As if it said to God, “Naught else I care for.” “Te lucis ante” so devoutly issued Forth from its mouth, and with such dulcet notes, It made me issue forth from my own mind. And then the others, sweetly and devoutly, Accompanied it through all the hymn entire, Having their eyes on the supernal wheels.

spans.t: Reflection

Late in the afternoon, a walking day changes its mind. The morning's resolve has been spent, the pack has been on for hours, and the end of the stage is near enough to think about but not near enough to touch. It is the hour when a mind with nothing to do turns for home: a kitchen, a voice, a particular chair. An hour ago you were not thinking of it, and now you can think of nothing else.

Dante knew that hour and wrote one of the best-loved sentences in the poem about it. It was the hour, he says, that turns back the desire of those who sail the sea, and melts their hearts on the day they have said farewell to their sweet friends. It is the hour that pierces the new pilgrim with love, if he hears from far away a bell that seems to grieve over the dying day. Two travellers are named: the sailor on his first day out, and the new pilgrim. Both have left something, and dusk shows them how much.
The word that matters is
new

. Not a pilgrim of years, but one in the first days, before the road has become a home. And the poem does not call the feeling a weakness or a fault. It does not tell him to ignore it. It says only that this is the hour: it comes at a certain time of day to those who have set out, and a bell from far away is enough to start it. You may never learn who is ringing it, or for what. It reaches you anyway.

What happens next is the part we hardly ever quote. Dante is in a small flowery valley at dusk, among a company of souls, and the poem turns from his own heart to theirs. One of them rises, joins his palms and lifts them, fixes his eyes on the east, and says to God, in words the poet puts in quotation marks,
Naught else I care for
. Then he sings an evening hymn, which the poem names only by its first Latin words,
Te lucis ante

, so devoutly and with such sweet notes that Dante is carried out of his own mind. The others join in, sweetly and devoutly, through the whole hymn, with their eyes on the heavens above them. Afterwards they look up in silence,
pale and humble
, as if waiting. Later in the canto two angels come down to guard the valley against a serpent that will arrive at night. Evening has its dangers, and the poem posts a watch.
It is a small, brave thing. At the very hour that melts the heart, someone stands up and sings, and the others follow.

What can you do about an hour like that? First, know it. If you know that the late afternoon is when the mind goes home, the feeling is less alarming. It is not a sign that the walk is wrong, or that you are weaker than the others, who may well be feeling it too. Second, to let the heart melt a little on purpose, and to name who is in it. Third, to give the feeling something to do. In the poem it is a hymn, sung together. For someone else it could be a message home, a pot of tea, a look at the sky, or three minutes of silence. Longing wants a shape. Without one it tends to sit in the chest and grow.

Two cautions. The first is that a hymn is not everyone's answer. We are not asking you to sing one, and nothing in this book depends on it. The point carries over to any kind of ending of the day: do something with your hands or your voice or your attention that says the day is closing, and say it in company if you can. The second runs the other way. A bell can start a spiral. The hour at the end of a stage is a poor time to decide whether to go on, because tiredness and longing make a very persuasive pair. Decide that after food and a night's sleep, when the light is better and the same question weighs less.
And
Naught else I care for

is a splendid sentence, though perhaps not one to say aloud at six in the evening to your blistered feet. It is a direction more than a report. The soul who says it has put everything down but one thing, and the day that is ending is what put it down for him.
You are reading this in the morning, and the hour is a long way off. Put it in your pocket, and let it be there when the bell rings.
For the walk

items.t: When the pull of home comes this afternoon, what will I do with it?

Notice the first time today that your mind turns for home. Say silently who or what it is. Walk three minutes with that person or place in mind, and then bring your attention back to the road. If you hear a bell, stop for as long as it rings, wherever you are, and let it be the whole of what you do.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If the bell hour came today, you have probably already met it, and if it did not, you were lucky or busy. Either way, you are now at the end of the day, which in this poem is the time when a whole company sings together.

Start with what the hour held. When did your mind turn for home, and what was in it? Perhaps a person, perhaps a room, perhaps something small, like the light through a particular window or the sound of a kettle. Notice that it was probably not what you would have guessed. Longing is a poor liar. It tells you quickly what you are carrying.

Then ask what you did with it. Did you push it down and walk faster? Did you sink into it and stop seeing the road? Or did you hold it for a few steps, as the poem's sailor and pilgrim hold it, and let it be true? Nobody gets this right the first time. The aim is only to notice the shape of your own habit, so that tomorrow's bell is a little less of a surprise.

Homesickness is a hard word, and not an accurate one. What you felt was love with a distance in it. That is not a flaw in the walking. It is evidence that there is something to go home to, and for some people that is the quiet news of the day. If there is nothing at home that pulls at you, that is true too, and worth a gentle thought. Someone might have been missing you all the same. Perhaps tonight is a good night for a short message, or a few lines in a notebook for someone who will read them later.

After the singing, the souls in the valley looked up in silence and waited. You can do something like that before you sleep. Sit for five minutes with nothing to read and nothing to do, and let the day settle. You may be too tired to feel anything much, and that is allowed. Strong feelings are louder when you are weary, and the same thought at noon would have weighed less.

The poem also posted a watch over its valley, so it is fair to ask what yours might be. The thing that comes at the end of a day is rarely a serpent. It is smaller: an old argument replayed, a worry about tomorrow built out of nothing, an hour lost to a screen. You might decide tonight, in advance, which of those you will not let in. A short list is enough, and it is easier to keep when you wrote it while you were calm.
One practical thing: deal with the small jobs first, such as socks, water and the phone on its charger. A tired mind that has things to do is less easily carried off by a bell.

items.t: When did my mind turn for home today, and what did it hold?
What did I do with that feeling, and what could I do with it tomorrow?
Who might like to hear from me, and what would I say to them in one line?

spans.t: A short prayer
For the ones I miss, thank you. Keep them well tonight, and keep me honest about what I feel. Let the bell at the end of the day be a kindness and not a wound. Give me a quiet mind and an easy sleep.

chapters.title: Day 4. Three steps and a gate

spans.t: What would it take to step through a door and not look back?
The passage

paras.t: Thither did we approach; and the first stair Was marble white, so polished and so smooth, I mirrored myself therein as I appear. The second, tinct of deeper hue than perse, Was of a calcined and uneven stone, Cracked all asunder lengthwise and across. The third, that uppermost rests massively, Porphyry seemed to me, as flaming red As blood that from a vein is spirting forth. … Devoutly at the holy feet I cast me, For mercy’s sake besought that he would open, But first upon my breast three times I smote. Seven P’s upon my forehead he described With the sword’s point, and, “Take heed that thou wash These wounds, when thou shalt be within,” he said. … Then pushed the portals of the sacred door, Exclaiming: “Enter; but I give you warning That forth returns whoever looks behind.”

spans.t: Reflection

Some thresholds on a road are real: a gate in a wall, a bridge, the sign at the edge of a town. You step through, and the place behind you stops being yours. Others you only notice afterwards, when you realise that somewhere in the last hour you stopped being a person who has just arrived and became a person who is walking.

Dante has been asleep. He wakes on the grass with the sun more than two hours high, frightened, not knowing where he is, and finds that only Virgil is beside him. His guide tells him what happened. At dawn, while Dante slept among the flowers, a lady came who said her name was Lucia.
So will I make his journey easier for him
, she said, and she carried him up the slope while he slept and set him down here. Ahead, where the cliff seems split, is the entrance.

It is worth stopping on that. In a book about climbing, the last stretch before the gate was not climbed by the climber. Some of the way is given. You may have a night's sleep that mends more than you expected, a meal that turns a day, or a stranger who points the right way before you ask. You cannot count on it, and you cannot earn it, and yet it is there in the poem, quietly, just before the gate.

Then the gate itself: a doorway in the rock, with three steps below it and a keeper seated at the top, whose face is more than the poet can bear. In his hand is a naked sword, which throws the sunbeams back so brightly that Dante keeps lifting his eyes in vain. The first step is white marble, polished so smooth that
I mirrored myself therein as I appear

. The second is dark, burnt, uneven stone, cracked right through, lengthwise and across. The third is red as blood from an opened vein. The keeper has his feet on this last, and he sits on a threshold that looks like diamond.

The poem does not say what the steps mean. Many readers have taken them as the stages of a change of heart: first, seeing yourself plainly; next, being broken open; last, a love hot enough to burn. That is one reading, and you may find another. But a walker can use the steps without a theory. The first is a mirror, and the oddest thing about it is the phrase
as I appear

, not worse and not better. The second is the crack: the plan that does not survive the first rain, the blister that tells you what the body cannot do. The third is heat, the thing that made you start.

Dante climbs them with his guide pulling him gently on, and kneels, and strikes his breast three times, and asks for mercy. The keeper takes the point of his sword and writes seven letters on Dante's forehead, each a P. On the usual reading, the P stands for the Latin word for sin, one for each ledge of the mountain, though the passage does not say so. He tells Dante to wash these wounds when he is inside. They are given as a task, not a sentence. Then the keeper takes out two keys, one gold and one silver, and opens the door. He says he has them from Peter, and that Peter told him to err on the side of opening rather than keeping shut, as long as people fall down at his feet.
The door is more generous than the warning that follows.
Enter; but I give you warning That forth returns whoever looks behind.

It is the one line in the passage that sounds like a trap, and we do not want to explain it away. But look at what it says. It does not say that the door locks. It says that whoever looks behind goes out again. On Day 2 the two travellers sat down on a ledge and looked back at the shore, and the poem called it a delight. The gate's warning is a different kind of looking: the glance of regret, the one that wishes you were still on the other side.

On the Camino nobody is forced onward. You can stop, you can take a bus, you can go home, and nobody should shame you for it. The poem is speaking of the heart and not the timetable. The question it puts to a walker is what you are leaving, and whether you can leave it without keeping one foot on the old side.
For the walk

items.t: What am I leaving at this gate, and can I leave it without a look of regret?

At the next doorway, gate, bridge or edge of a village, stop for one breath. Name, silently, one thing you are leaving behind: a worry, a plan, a version of yourself. Step through and walk to the next bend before you look back. When you do look, look at the view, not at the thing you left.

spans.t: At the end of the day

A day has more doors in it than you notice. The one you went out of this morning, the first step onto the road, the door of the place where you ate, and the door of the place where you are sitting now. Each time you passed one you were a little different on the other side.

You could do what the first step did, and look at yourself. If there is a mirror where you are staying, even a small one over a basin, look into it for a full minute. If there is none, a dark window will do. Not to judge the face, and not to flatter it. Let it show you the day as it appears: the colour, the lines about the eyes, the dust at the hairline. The step in the poem is
so polished and so smooth
that Dante sees himself exactly. See what you can bear to see.

Then the second step, the crack. Something broke or bent today. A plan, a pace, a mood, a hope about how a stage would go. Say what it was. A crack is information, and information is more useful than a sealed surface.

And the third, the red. What was warm today? Something is the reason you set out, and some days you can feel it and some days you cannot. If you could feel it today, give it its due. If not, it has not gone.

One more thing from the passage, the oldest kindness in it. Dante was carried while he slept. Think of what carried you today without your doing: the sleep, a meal that arrived on time, a word from a stranger, a stretch of road that was gentler than the map suggested. You may be too tired to be grateful, and that is all right. It is enough to notice it, as you would a hand under your elbow on a stair. If you looked back with regret at something today, it is also enough to say so, without making a case.

The keeper told Dante to wash his marks once he was inside, and washing is the sort of work that gets done in small amounts, again and again. Tonight's portion might be literal: warm water over tired feet, a face rinsed twice. It might also be one thing to let go of, a sharp word said to someone or a mean thought you had about a stranger. You do not have to rehearse it. Name it, and let the water have it.

Tomorrow will open with a door of its own, the one of the room you are in now. You might decide tonight what you will leave in it. Whatever the evening has taught you, you do not have to carry all of it out.

items.t: When I looked at myself plainly today, what did I see?
What did I try to leave behind, and how often did I look back at it?
What carried me today that I did not do for myself?

spans.t: A short prayer

Open the door a little wider than I expect. Let me see myself plainly and not turn away. Wash what needs washing, and do it gently. Carry me where my legs cannot. Let me go on without a look over my shoulder.

chapters.title: Day 5. The weight on the back

spans.t: How much of what you carry is for the road, and how much is for show?
The passage

paras.t: “The grievous quality Of this their torment bows them so to earth, That my own eyes at first contended with it; But look there fixedly, and disentangle By sight what cometh underneath those stones; Already canst thou see how each is stricken.” … As to sustain a ceiling or a roof, In place of corbel, oftentimes a figure Is seen to join its knees unto its breast, Which makes of the unreal real anguish Arise in him who sees it, fashioned thus Beheld I those, when I had ta’en good heed. True is it, they were more or less bent down, According as they more or less were laden; And he who had most patience in his looks Weeping did seem to say, “I can no more!”

spans.t: Reflection

Lift your pack at six in the morning and it tells you the truth about yesterday's packing. The straps bite where they bit before. Something in there you have not touched since you set out is still riding on your hips. You may find yourself weighing every item in your mind, the book, the second pair of shoes, the thing you brought just in case, and deciding what you could do without.
The first ledge of the mountain is the ledge of pride, and its picture is a weight. The two travellers come out of a narrow crack in the rock onto a wide shelf, a plain
more desolate than roads across the deserts

, with a wall of white marble on the inner side. The wall is carved with scenes so alive that Dante thinks the angel of the Annunciation is about to say his greeting. There is a king dancing in front of the holy ark, and his wife watching from a palace window with scorn. And there is an emperor, Trajan, riding out with his cavalry, who is stopped by a poor widow standing at his bridle. Her son has been killed, and she wants justice. He tells her to wait until he returns. And if he does not return? she asks. Whoever sits in his place will do it, he says. What good is another's good deed to him, she says, if he neglects his own? And the emperor tells her to take comfort: he must do his duty before he moves, because justice wills it, and pity holds him back.

It is a curious image for the ledge of the proud. The great man who stops. Each of the three scenes shows someone who put their own importance down for a moment, and the carvings run along the wall where the souls will pass.

The souls themselves do not appear until Dante has looked his fill. Then he sees something coming towards them that does not look like people, and asks what it is. The torment of these figures bows them so low to the earth, Virgil answers, that his own eyes at first argued with the sight. Look hard, and
disentangle By sight what cometh underneath those stones

. They are not strange creatures. They are people carrying boulders, and each is bent according to the size of the stone. The poet compares them to the carved figures that hold up a roof or a ceiling in some old building, with knees drawn to the chest. Such a figure, he says, makes an unreal pain real in whoever watches it. And then comes the line that stays with the reader:
he who had most patience in his looks Weeping did seem to say, “I can no more!”

The one who says it is the most patient. The strongest person on the ledge, the one who has borne it best, is at the end of what he can do. The poem gives no help to the story that toughness is the answer.
What is pride, on a road? It is not only arrogance. It is the
I'm fine

when you are not, the refusal of a lift of the arm or a plaster, the extra kilometre taken so as not to be the one who stopped, the carrying of more than you need so that nobody will think you unprepared. It is heavy for a simple reason: the effort of keeping up an appearance is a weight, and it bends you away from what is in front of you, which on this ledge is the ground. And notice that the stones come in different sizes. Each person is bent
according as they more or less were laden
. Nobody else can tell how heavy your load is. That is a good reason not to guess at theirs.

Two things need saying. First, the picture is severe, and we do not want to hide that. A reader may well flinch at stones as a penalty. One way to read it is as the image of what pride already is, and not as a punishment added from outside: a heavy thing, slow to bear, that makes it hard to see anyone else. Second, there is a good kind of pride, in a day well walked or a hard job done, and the poem is not speaking of that. Its pride is the other kind, the one that needs to be above someone.

Two small practices come out of the wall and the stones. Ask for one small help, or accept one that is offered, without a speech. And stop for one person who stands in your way, as the emperor stopped for the widow. You will not carry less because of it. You may well stand straighter.
For the walk

items.t: What am I carrying today in order to look strong?

Ask for one small help or accept one that is offered: directions, a hand with a strap, a mouthful of water. Say thank you, and leave out the excuse. And if someone speaks to you while you are hurrying, stop for as long as the conversation lasts. Afterwards, notice whether your shoulders have dropped.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Shoes off, straps off. Whatever the stones were today, you have put them down for the night, and the first thing the body does is tell you how much it carried. Let it. Roll your shoulders, loosen your hips, and give the places where the pack sat a chance to breathe. If the straps have rubbed anything raw, look at it: clean it, dry it, cover it. If it is more than a rub, ask at a pharmacy.
Then look back for the
I'm fine

. Most of us said it at least once. To a person who offered something, to a companion who asked how the feet were, to ourselves at the foot of a hill. It is such a small sentence. Where did it come out of your mouth today, and what was it protecting? You do not need to scold yourself. Pride is common and it is tiring, and the first step towards putting it down is to notice where it sits.

Sort the load, too, in the mind if not yet in the pack. Some of what you carry today is the body's real need: water, a layer for the cold, a plaster. Some of it is not. It may be an item you took out and put back three times because you could not bring yourself to leave it. It may be an idea of how fast you ought to be, or a picture of how you look. Which weight was real? You do not have to decide tonight, and it is no moment for big choices when you are tired. A note to yourself is enough: that one, tomorrow, I will not carry.
There is a sentence in the passage that is not only for the proud.
I can no more.

At nine o'clock at night it is simply an accurate report, and the answer to it is sleep, not a pep talk. If you said it today, even to yourself, you were not failing at the road. You were telling the truth about a body that has done a day's work.

Look round the room, too, if you are among other people. Everyone has put their stones down, and no two loads were the same. You cannot see the size of another person's day, only its effect: the way someone sits, or the care with which they take off a boot. If somebody near you looks more bent than you would expect, a small kindness costs little. A plaster, a glass of water, a seat moved along a bench.

Think, finally, of the person who stopped you today, or the one you stopped for. A greeting, a question, a person who needed a hand with a map. Was it a nuisance or was it the best part of the day? The emperor in the carving is not made smaller by the widow.

items.t: Where did I say I was fine today when I was not?
What am I carrying that is for the road, and what is only for show?
Who stopped for me today, or whom did I stop for?

spans.t: A short prayer
Let me put down what was never mine to carry. Teach me to ask, and to take what is offered without a speech. Make my back honest and my load small. Let whoever is bent beside me be lifted too.

chapters.title: Day 6. Daily bread and a breath of wind

spans.t: What do you need for today, and what do you only want to be known for?
The passage

paras.t: Give unto us this day our daily manna, Withouten which in this rough wilderness Backward goes he who toils most to advance. … Here of such pride is paid the forfeiture; And yet I should not be here, were it not That, having power to sin, I turned to God. … O thou vain glory of the human powers, How little green upon thy summit lingers, If’t be not followed by an age of grossness! In painting Cimabue thought that he Should hold the field, now Giotto has the cry, So that the other’s fame is growing dim. … Naught is this mundane rumour but a breath Of wind, that comes now this way and now that, And changes name, because it changes side.

spans.t: Reflection

The first meal of a walking day is easy to rush: a coffee on your feet, something sweet in your pocket, and out. It does not feel like an important decision. But a good deal of the day is settled at that bar counter, or on that bench, in the next ten minutes.

The souls on the ledge of the proud have no bar and no bench. They walk bent under their stones, and as they go they say a prayer aloud, which Dante gives in a long version of the Lord's Prayer, said for themselves and, as the poem says, for us. The passage opens with one line of it:
Give unto us this day our daily manna.

Manna was the food that fell in the desert, in the Bible, for the people who were wandering there, enough for one day at a time. The poem turns the petition into something plain and almost brusque. Without it, it says, in this rough wilderness, the one who toils hardest to get ahead goes backward.

That is a very practical sentence to find in a prayer. It describes a person who is trying hard and failing to advance, and puts the cause where the person would least expect it: not in a lack of effort but in a lack of bread. A walker may know this. The most determined are often the ones who skip the stop, the water and the proper meal, and then lose the afternoon. The word that matters is
daily
. Not enough for the week, not enough for the whole of the road, only today's, and then tomorrow's again.

The prayer ends, in the poem, with a request that is not for the speakers. They say they need no protection for themselves, so the last words are for the sake of those who have been left behind. These are bent, weighed-down people, and their last breath of prayer goes to someone else.

Then one of them twists under his stone and looks up at Dante, who has been walking bowed beside them, and calls him by name. He is Oderisi, a painter of manuscript pages from Gubbio (Agobbio, in the translation), who was once much admired. He says the pages painted by another man, Franco, now outshine his own, and the honour is mostly Franco's. And he adds, with honesty, that he would not have been so gracious while he lived, because of the great desire for excellence on which his heart was set. It cost him a place on this ledge. And yet, he says, he would not be here at all had he not turned to God while he still had the power to sin.

Then he speaks of fame. Vain glory, he says, keeps so little green on its summit, unless a dull age comes after. Cimabue thought he held the field in painting, and now Giotto has the cry, and Cimabue's fame grows dim. They were painters of Dante's own day, one after the other, and each was the best in his time. And then the line that is the core of the passage:
Naught is this mundane rumour but a breath Of wind, that comes now this way and now that, And changes name, because it changes side.

Hold the picture a moment. A wind that changes name when it changes side. The reputation you have is not in you; it is in the way the air is moving at the moment, and it is called something different tomorrow. Put beside the bread, it makes a pair. One is what you need to keep going. The other is what you would like to be thought of while you do it.

A road lends itself to scoring. There are the kilometres, the early starts, the weight of the pack, the stage you did when others stopped, and the story you are already composing for the people at home. None of this is bad in itself. But it is wind, and the more of it you carry, the more you lean.

A pair of qualifications. First, Oderisi is not saying that excellence is a sin. The poem calls him the honour of his art, and the wish to do a thing well is a good wish. What he regrets is the need to be first, which turns a craft into a contest. Second, there is a joke in the passage, whether or not the poet meant it. The speaker of this lecture on the shortness of fame is a character in a poem that has been read for some seven centuries, and that has helped keep his name in circulation. Reputation may be a breath of wind, but some breaths last longer than others.
In practice: eat, drink and rest as if your progress depended on it, because it does. And when someone overtakes you, let them go with your good wishes and not your arithmetic.
For the walk

items.t: What do I actually need for today?
When someone overtakes you, say
Buen Camino

and mean it, without checking how fast they are going or how light their pack looks. If you overtake someone, do the same. See how long you can go today without comparing yourself to anyone at all, and notice what the day feels like when you do.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Supper is the day's own manna, the bread that came for today. If you are at a table with other people, notice how rarely the food is the interesting part, and how often it is the thing that lets the talking start. If you are eating alone, eat as if it mattered, because it does. A day's walking is paid for, in part, at this hour.

Was it enough? Did you take the bread when it was offered, or did you skip the stop at midday and arrive hungry and cross? Be practical about it. There is no virtue in running on empty. The poem puts the cost plainly: even the hardest worker goes backward without it.

Now the wind. Go through the day and find the comparisons. Almost everybody makes them, and they are rarely deliberate. The person who walked faster, who had the lighter pack, who knew the language, who seemed to be enjoying it more. What did the comparing cost you? Perhaps nothing, and perhaps an hour of the afternoon. Comparison cuts in both directions, too. On some days you feel above somebody, and that is the same wind, blowing from the other side.

It may help to remember how little of this travels. Tomorrow you will be among people who do not know what you did today, and nobody in the next village will have heard of your stage. That can be a relief. A road is one of the few places where reputation does not follow you, and you are free to be plain.

Remember, too, where the passage's prayer ended: with those who stayed behind. Somebody at home may be thinking of you tonight, or may have meant to. The souls on the ledge spend their last words on people who are not there. You might do the same for a minute. Name two or three of them, and wish them a good night, whether or not you pray.

And what praise did you want today? Most of us want some, at the end of a hard day, and it is honest to admit it. The question is whether you needed it or only wanted it. Needing it is human. Wanting it is only wind, but it pulls hard when you are tired, and it is better to know the pull by name.

Try a small test. Imagine telling the story of today tomorrow, at a table with strangers. What would you leave out, and what would you polish? There is nothing sinister in it, since everyone edits. But the day as it was, with its bread and its sulks and its sore heel, is better company than the day as it will be told.
If you are too tired for any of this, leave it. A meal, a wash and a bed are a good evening's work, and the questions will keep until tomorrow. They are not an examination.

items.t: Did I take today's bread, and was it enough?
Whom did I measure myself against today, and what did the measuring cost?
What praise did I want today that I could have done without?

spans.t: A short prayer
Give me today's bread and not tomorrow's worry. Keep my eyes off other people's pace, and let the credit for what I do be small. Bless the ones who passed me and the ones I passed.
Who is holding up whom, and who has noticed?
The passage

paras.t: And even as I asked, behold the third, Saying: “Love those from whom ye have had evil!” … Covered with sackcloth vile they seemed to me, And one sustained the other with his shoulder, And all of them were by the bank sustained. Thus do the blind, in want of livelihood, Stand at the doors of churches asking alms, And one upon another leans his head, So that in others pity soon may rise, Not only at the accent of their words, But at their aspect, which no less implores. … “O brother mine, each one is citizen Of one true city; but thy meaning is, Who may have lived in Italy a pilgrim.”

spans.t: Reflection

Look at a rest stop in the middle of a morning. A low wall in the shade, a row of packs leaning against it, and people leaning against the packs. Nobody has arranged it. Shoulders touch because the wall is only so long and the shade only so wide, and for ten minutes nobody minds. It is one of the plainest sights on any long road, and it is a picture the second ledge of the mountain can make something of.

The ledge of envy is bare. The poem says there is no shade and no carving, only the dull blue-grey of the stone. Virgil stops, uncertain, and does something unexpected for a guide: he turns to the sun and asks it to lead.
Thou warmest the world, thou shinest over it

, he says, and the two travellers cover a mile in no time. Then voices go past them in the air, unseen, calling out examples of generous love. The third of them is a command, and it opens our passage:
Love those from whom ye have had evil!
Virgil tells Dante that this ledge punishes envy, and that the lashes of its whip are made from love.

Then they see the souls. They are sitting against the cliff, in coarse cloaks the colour of the rock, so that at first the stone seems to have people in it. The poet compares them to blind beggars at the doors of churches, asking alms, with one resting his head against another's, so that pity will rise in the passer-by,
Not only at the accent of their words, But at their aspect, which no less implores.
These souls prop each other by the shoulder, and the bank props them all.

They are blind for a reason the poem gives without softening. An iron wire runs through their eyelids and sews them shut, as a hawk's are sewn to keep it still. Dante, passing, is uneasy. He sees them and they cannot see him, and it feels like an outrage, so he turns to Virgil, who knows what he wants before he says it and tells him to speak, and to be brief.
He speaks to them. If any of them is Italian, he asks. And a voice answers, gently, with the sentence we have in our passage:
O brother mine, each one is citizen Of one true city; but thy meaning is, Who may have lived in Italy a pilgrim.

It is a quiet correction that is also a rebuke to envy. Everyone here belongs to one true city, the voice says. What you mean is someone who lived in Italy as a pilgrim. So a whole human life is a pilgrimage, and a country is only a stretch of the road. In the poem's own faith, the city is heaven. For another reader it may simply mean the one human road.

Dante goes towards the voice, and the soul he finds there, a woman from Siena, goes on to say something terrible about herself, in a few lines we do not quote: that she was happier at another's misfortune than at her own good luck. It is a very exact description of envy. It is not hunger for what the other person has, but a flicker of gladness when they lose it.

On a road, envy is small. It is the person with the lighter pack, the knees that do not hurt, the last bed taken by someone who came in a minute earlier. It is another walker's photographs, or his ease with the language, or the friends he seems to have found already. It lasts a few seconds, and then we are annoyed with ourselves for having felt it. It is embarrassing, and the embarrassment makes it hard to look at.

The poem's answer is odd, and worth sitting with. It does not take the envious and make them stronger, or better at winning. It shuts their eyes, so that they cannot look sideways, and then it makes them lean on each other. The cure for the sideways look is to need someone, and to be seen needing. A group that is propping itself up has little room for a contest.

Two places in this passage are hard. First, the wire is a grim image, and a reader may reasonably think it too much. We would say only that the poem's pictures of punishment are mirrors of the fault: the eyes that were always looking at others are now closed. Second,
Love those from whom ye have had evil

is a hard command. It is not advice on forgiving someone who has asked. It is a voice from the air, and the poem does not pretend it is easy. On a road it may be small: the person who pushed in at the water tap, or snored all night. You are not asked to feel anything. You are asked, perhaps, to wish them well once.

The day's task, then, is to lean and to be leant on. To take the shoulder that is offered, and to be one. And when the sideways look comes, to answer it with a small, silent good wish for the person you are looking at.
For the walk

items.t: Whose good luck do I find hard to watch today?

When envy twitches, give that person one silent good wish, in a sentence of your own, and mean it as much as you can. If you are able, do something small for someone: hold a gate, share a map, pass the water. Notice whether the twitch has gone, and do it again the next time it comes.

spans.t: At the end of the day

There is a place in the poem where a whole ledge of people are propped by the person beside them and by the wall. Tonight, take a moment to find the wall in your own day. Who held you up? It may have been a companion, or a stranger with directions, or a shopkeeper who said something kind. It may have been a bench, or a tree trunk, or the plain fact of a road that other people have walked before you.

And who did you hold up? Almost everyone has been somebody's shoulder today without knowing it: a word at the right moment, a share of something, a place made on a bench. You do not need a list. It is enough to know it is true.

Now the sideways look. Did you meet it today? It is worth looking at it calmly now, at the end of the day, because it is smaller than it seemed. Think of one moment when you envied someone. Look at what it was really about. The envy is often a pointer, and it points less to the person than to something in you that wants attention. The lighter pack points to a wish for ease. The faster pace points to a fear of being less able than you hoped. Once you see that, you can be kinder to both people, the one you envied and the one who felt it.

There is something else the poem notices, in Dante's own shame. He walks past people who cannot see him, and he finds it awkward to look at them. It is a good instinct. Today, did you look at anyone who did not know it: a stranger asleep on a bench, someone limping, a person talking quietly into a phone? There is a courtesy in looking away. There is another in looking, and seeing whether a hand is needed.

Think, last of all, of the people in the room tonight, or at the next table. They are all on their way to the same city, and some of them you will never see again. If you can, say one good word to somebody before the light goes out. It costs nothing, and envy is hard to keep up against it.

Turn it round, once. Somebody may have looked at you today with that small twitch: for your lighter boots, your companion, your easy stride, a bed you were lucky to get. It is hard to imagine from the inside, because you know what the day cost you. A little care costs nothing, and the best answer to a sideways look is to be easy to be near.
If envy was loud today, note that it is louder when you are hungry or tired. That is not an excuse, only a fact, and a reason to eat and sleep.

items.t: Whose good luck did I find hard to watch today, and what did it show me that I want?
Who held me up today, in any way at all?
Whose shoulder could I be tomorrow?

spans.t: A short prayer

Keep my eyes from the sideways look. Let me lean without shame and be leant on without complaint. Bless the ones I envied today, and give me what I truly need. Make me glad at other people's luck, even if I learn it slowly.
What do you do when anger takes the view away?
The passage

paras.t: Darkness of hell, and of a night deprived Of every planet under a poor sky, As much as may be tenebrous with cloud, Ne’er made unto my sight so thick a veil, As did that smoke which there enveloped us, Nor to the feeling of so rough a texture; For not an eye it suffered to stay open; Whereat mine escort, faithful and sagacious, Drew near to me and offered me his shoulder. E’en as a blind man goes behind his guide, Lest he should wander, or should strike against Aught that may harm or peradventure kill him, So went I through the bitter and foul air, Listening unto my Leader, who said only, “Look that from me thou be not separated.” … “Thee will I follow far as is allowed me,” He answered; “and if smoke prevent our seeing, Hearing shall keep us joined instead thereof.” … Remember, Reader, if e’er in the Alps A mist o’ertook thee, through which thou couldst see Not otherwise than through its membrane mole, How, when the vapours humid and condensed Begin to dissipate themselves, the sphere Of the sun feebly enters in among them, And thy imagination will be swift In coming to perceive how I re-saw The sun at first, that was already setting. Thus, to the faithful footsteps of my Master Mating mine own, I issued from that cloud To rays already dead on the low shores.

cite.t: ), Cantos XVI and XVII (tr. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow)

spans.t: Reflection

Mist does something strange to a road. The next marker vanishes, then the next bend, and the world shrinks to a few metres of path with a wall of white on every side. Sounds seem nearer. You find yourself staying close to whoever is ahead, or you stop talking, or you slow down without being told to. If you have ever been caught in cloud on a hill, you know the particular quiet of it.

Anger does the same thing, only on the inside. In the middle of it you cannot see the other person, or the day, or the way out, and the world is the size of the grievance. The third ledge of the mountain is the ledge of the angry, and the poem's picture of it is smoke.

The passage begins with a fierce description of darkness. Neither the darkness of hell, Dante says, nor a night without a single planet under a poor, cloud-choked sky, ever made so thick a veil as this smoke, or one so rough to the feeling. It does not even allow an eye to stay open. So Virgil, faithful and wise, draws close and offers his shoulder, and Dante goes after him as a blind man goes behind his guide, to keep from wandering or striking something that might harm or kill him. All Virgil says is:
Look that from me thou be not separated.

Inside the smoke there are voices, and they are singing. In the lines we skip, they all sing the same words in the same measure, a prayer for mercy and peace, so that harmony seems to hold among them even though no one can see anyone. Then a voice asks who this is that cuts through their smoke as if he still reckoned the days by the calendar. It belongs to a man who says his name is Marco, a Lombard, who loved the world's excellence, and who agrees to go with them as far as he is allowed. And he says the sentence that is the heart of this day:
and if smoke prevent our seeing, Hearing shall keep us joined instead thereof.

If you cannot see, listen. It is a very simple instruction and a rarely used one. Sight is the sense we trust, and anger shuts it first, so we blunder on trusting it. The poem proposes a different thread: a voice, a presence, a sound that stays beside you. Marco goes on to speak of the world's troubles, and we will not follow him. But he stays with the travellers while the smoke lasts, and that is what the passage is for.
Then the poet turns to you.
Remember, Reader, if e'er in the Alps A mist o'ertook thee.

He is addressing a walker, someone who has been caught on a mountain. He asks you to recall how it felt when the thick vapours begin to thin and the sun enters among them weakly, and he says your imagination will be quick to understand how he first saw the sun again. He does not describe it. He trusts yours. And look at what he saw: the sun was already setting. They come out of the smoke into rays
already dead on the low shores

It is not noon after the anger. It is a late, low light, and it is enough to walk by. That is honest. Some anger clears at midday, and some only as the day is closing, and you cannot hurry it. You can only keep your hand on the shoulder and wait for the vapour to thin.

Three limits on all this. First, the poem does not say that every anger is wrong. Elsewhere on this ledge it shows quiet examples of gentleness. The ledge is for the anger that has become blind, which is another matter. Second, there is no cure here for the real wrong that may lie behind a person's anger. A grievance can be just and the smoke still smothering. Third, you cannot always stay close to a guide. Sometimes there is nobody, and you are in the smoke with your own thoughts. Then the thread may be your own voice, saying one short sentence aloud, or the plain count of your own steps.

On the Camino, the causes are small and ordinary: a missed turn, a snorer, a person ahead who walks at the wrong speed, a bar that has run out of what you wanted, your own tired body. By mid-afternoon you may be in it already.

So, today: notice when the view narrows. Stop talking, for a hundred steps if you can. Listen for something that holds: the sea, a bell, a footstep behind you, the person beside you. And let the late sun count as the sun.
For the walk

items.t: When my view narrows, what can I still hear?

When you notice irritation rising, stop talking and keep silent for a hundred steps. Listen: to your feet, your breath, the wind, water, a bell, a voice in the distance. Speak again only if the words are still needed. If you are walking with someone, tell them in advance that you will do this, so that the silence is not a message.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If you met the smoke today, you will know it by the smell it leaves on the evening. Even when the vapour has gone, a day that had anger in it keeps some of the sourness. So open the window, or sit near a door, and let a little air in.

Begin with the cause, and keep it small. Name the thing that did it, in one or two words. A person, a delay, a pain, a sound. You may find that it was not what you were angry about at the time. Fatigue, hunger and thirst are cheap sources of fury, and a surprising number of rows are settled by a sandwich. That is not an excuse, only a useful thing to know.

Then think about what you did inside it. Did you speak, or go silent, or walk faster? Did you hold on to someone, a companion or a voice, or did you try to find the way alone? In the poem the guide offers his shoulder and the only instruction is to keep in touch. Whose presence kept you joined to the day, even when you could not see well? It may have been very quiet. A person who said nothing and walked beside you has done what Virgil did.

Anger at yourself is also smoke. A wrong turn, a forgotten item, a decision you regret: these cloud the eyes in the same way, and they are harder to talk your way out of, because nobody else is to blame. If that was your smoke today, the poem's answer is the same: stay close to what is good in you, and listen to it. Be as gentle with yourself as you would be with someone you were guiding.

And if you said a sharp word to somebody, or kept a cold silence that was meant to be heard, the end of the day is a good time to mend it. A sentence is enough: that you were short with them, and are sorry. If you were right, and still unkind, you can be sorry for the unkindness alone. If you cannot do it tonight, do it in the morning, before the road has started to set.

If you tried the hundred steps of silence this morning, think about what you heard in them. For most people it is something ordinary, such as their own feet and breath, a gate, birdsong, a distant engine, and it is usually more than they expected. That small, steady sound is the thread the poem is talking about, and it is always there, even on a day when you did not need it.
If there is a sunset where you are, and it is safe to look at it, go and see it. The poem's late sun is a good one to end with.

items.t: When did my view narrow today, and what did I do about it?
Whose voice or presence kept me joined to the road?
Is there a sharp word I could soften with a single sentence?

spans.t: A short prayer

When the smoke comes, let me hear a voice. Keep a hand on my shoulder and a guard on my tongue. Let the sun come back low and gentle, and let me walk by it. Forgive what I said in the dark, and teach me to be quiet sooner.
Is the trouble your legs, or the warmth of your love for the road?
The passage

paras.t: The love of good, remiss In what it should have done, is here restored; Here plied again the ill-belated oar; … Full soon they were upon us, because running Moved onward all that mighty multitude, And two in the advance cried out, lamenting, “Mary in haste unto the mountain ran, And Caesar, that he might subdue Ilerda, Thrust at Marseilles, and then ran into Spain.” “Quick! quick! so that the time may not be lost By little love!” forthwith the others cried, “For ardour in well-doing freshens grace!” … So full of longing are we to move onward, That stay we cannot; therefore pardon us, If thou for churlishness our justice take.

cite.t: ), Cantos XVII and XVIII (tr. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow)

spans.t: Reflection

There is a stretch near the end of most walking days that has nothing wrong with it, and is still the hardest. It is the last third of a stage. You are not injured and you are not exhausted. You have simply gone flat. A bench with a view becomes twenty minutes, then forty. The next kilometre does not look like anything you want. The poem has a word for this condition, and it gives a surprising definition of it.
It comes at nightfall on the mountain. Dante and his guide have climbed the stairs to the fourth ledge, and as the sun goes down Dante finds that his legs have simply stopped.
O manhood mine, why dost thou vanish so?

he says to himself, and the stairs end, and they halt like a ship that has reached the shore. Then he asks Virgil what fault is purged here, and Virgil replies, and the answer is the first lines of our passage. The love of good, he says, that was slack in what it should have done is here restored. Here the oar that was taken up too late is plied again.

That is the definition. Sloth in the poem is not tiredness, and it is not a slow body. It is slack love: a good thing loved too faintly, so that the rowing is put off. The fault is in the warmth, not in the legs.

What follows is nearly comic. A crowd comes running along the ledge, all of them, a great multitude in a hurry. Two at the front cry out as they run, and what they cry are examples of haste. The first is Mary, who in the Gospel goes in a hurry up into the hill country to see her cousin. The second is Caesar, who attacked Marseilles and then ran into Spain to win a war. Behind them, others call:
Quick! quick! so that the time may not be lost By little love!
and then
For ardour in well-doing freshens grace!

Dante's guide stops them, politely, and asks the way up. One of them calls over his shoulder to follow them and the opening will be found. They are so full of longing to go on, he says, that they cannot stop, and he begs pardon in case it looks like rudeness. And off they go. Behind them, near the end of the crowd, two more shout their warnings, about people who gave up before the end of a long journey and settled for a life without glory.
Consider what drives them. It is not a whip. Their cry is against
little love
, and the reason they run is that they are
So full of longing
. The speed is a symptom, not an order. They go fast because they want to, as someone hurries towards a person who is waiting for them. Hurry here is a sign of warmth.
So the flat patch of an afternoon may be cold love more than tired legs. You have forgotten why you want to be here, or you have never quite said it. The remedy is not a faster pace. It is a reason.

We should say plainly what the passage does not mean. It is not an order to hurry on the Camino. The road is long, and rushing in the first week is one of the quickest ways of failing it. Earlier in the poem the same travellers sit down on a ledge, and it does not object. In the poem,
quick
means willing. Your pace is yours.

Nor is tiredness the same as sloth. A body that has walked for eight hours is rightly spent, and the poem does not rebuke it. Dante himself stops at dusk with his legs, in the poem's phrase, in truce, and Virgil lets him. How do you tell the difference? Here is one test, and it is only one. If someone you loved were waiting at the end of the next kilometre, would you find the legs? If you would, the legs are better than you thought, and the trouble is warmth. If you would not, rest.

One more thing is worth admitting. Warmth does not come on request, and the poem knows that, because its runners are given their longing and do not manufacture it. But you can give the walking a reason, and a small reason is enough. A person, a view, a destination, the next village's name, the colour of the sea at the next bend. Plying the oar again does not have to mean pulling hard. A slow step with some love in it may be worth more than a fast one without.
For today, then: find one reason for the next kilometre, and say it. And if you must stop, stop for a reason, and stand up for one too.
For the walk

items.t: Is this tiredness, or has my love for the road gone lukewarm?

At the first flat patch of the afternoon, give the next kilometre a reason: a person to walk it for, or something particular to look for, a bird, a doorway, the colour of the water. Carry that reason to the end of the kilometre, then choose another, or rest.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Somewhere between lunch and the end of the stage there was probably a slump, and tonight is a good time to look at it kindly. When did you go flat, and where were you? Remember the place, if you can.
