And what happened? Did you stop? Did something move you on: a person, a hill, a bar, a bell, the plain thought of a bed?

The test from this morning is worth trying on the afternoon in hindsight. Was it your legs, or was it your love? Legs give signs of their own: heaviness that does not lift, a particular ache, a trembling. Love gives different ones: boredom, a dull what is the point, a reaching for the phone, a wish for the day to be over. You will come to know your own signs, and it may take a few evenings. Neither is wrong. Only the reading of them is worth getting right.

Before you decide which kind of flat it was, check the dull basics. Had you drunk enough, and eaten since the morning? Was there a damp sock, or a stone in a boot? A great deal of lukewarmness turns out to be a missing glass of water. The poem's definition is a deep one, but the first step in telling love from legs is to feed the legs.

Look for the warm moments, too. The runners in the poem are cheerful in a ragged way, and you may have had a few such moments yourself, even on a flat day. A coffee at the right time, a view that stopped you, a moment of talk, a dog that came to say hello. Note two or three of them. They are the fuel the next day will run on, and they are easy to forget by morning.

Think of anyone whose pace pulled you along today: a companion, or someone a little ahead on the path whom you followed for a while without ever speaking. The runners in the poem carry one another along without a word. Such a person may never know what they did for you. You can thank them in your mind.

Did hurry pass itself off as love today? It is easy to confuse the two. Moving fast to get to the end is not the same as wanting to be on the road. The poem's runners go fast for love. If you went fast for any other reason, you may have missed some of what was there.

And on the days when there was no warmth at all, and you walked on from habit alone, that is allowed. Turning up, again, without ardour, is a form of love of its own. The poem has a place for the quick, and it does not despise those who take their time.
Lay the oar down now. It will be there in the morning.

items.t: When did I go flat today, and was it my legs or my love?
What gave the next kilometre a reason?
What, however small, made me glad to be on this road?

spans.t: A short prayer

Warm what has gone cold in me. Give me a reason for the next kilometre, and a slow step with some love in it. Forgive the hours I only waited for the day to end. Let me lay the oar down tonight. In the morning, let me take it up again.
What are your eyes fastened on, and what are you missing while they are?
The passage

paras.t: On the fifth circle when I had come forth, People I saw upon it who were weeping, Stretched prone upon the ground, all downward turned. “Adhaesit pavimento anima mea,” I heard them say with sighings so profound, That hardly could the words be understood. … Even as our eye did not uplift itself Aloft, being fastened upon earthly things, So justice here has merged it in the earth. … I on my knees had fallen, and wished to speak; But even as I began, and he was ’ware, Only by listening, of my reverence, “What cause,” he said, “has downward bent thee thus?” And I to him: “For your own dignity, Standing, my conscience stung me with remorse.” “Straighten thy legs, and upward raise thee, brother,” … Err not, fellow-servant am I With thee and with the others to one power.

spans.t: Reflection

On a rough track you have to look at your feet. The stones are loose, the roots are waiting, and a twisted ankle is a long way from anywhere. Looking down is simply good sense, and a day's walking is mostly done that way. But there is another kind of looking down, which has nothing to do with the path. It happens when the eyes are fixed on the pack, the phone, the count of kilometres, the cost of the next bed, the thing you wish you had bought. It is easy to spend a whole afternoon there, and to arrive with no memory of the hills.

The fifth ledge of the mountain is built on that kind of looking. Dante and Virgil climb up onto it and find people lying flat on the ground, face down, weeping. They are saying a line in Latin from the Psalms,
Adhaesit pavimento anima mea

, which means roughly, my soul clings to the ground, and they sigh so deeply that the words can hardly be made out. When Virgil asks the way, they tell him to keep to the outside. Dante goes up to one of them, and the voice that answers is an old one.

He says, in Latin, that he was a successor of Peter, which is to say a pope. He held the office for a little more than a month, and in that time he found out how heavy the great cloak is on whoever keeps it out of the mud. Every other burden, he says, seems a feather beside it. And he discovered that life is a lie: that there was nothing further to climb, and that the heart is not at rest there. Until then, he says, he had been a wretched soul, parted from God and wholly avaricious.

Then comes the explanation of the ledge, and our passage gives its first lines. Even as our eye did not lift itself, being fastened on earthly things, so justice here has pressed it into the earth. A little later he adds that, because avarice had put out our love for every good, so that action was lost, justice now holds them bound by the feet and hands, until it pleases the Lord to let them go. The punishment is the habit made visible. They looked at the ground all their lives, and now they look at nothing else.
One phrase deserves a pause:
whereby was action lost.

In the poem, avarice does more than make a person grasping. It stops them. Someone who clutches things gets nothing done with them. The hand that closes around a possession cannot be used to do anything else, and the same is true of the eyes.

Then comes the part of the story that moves the reader. Dante, who is alive and who has just heard a pope, falls on his knees. He wants to speak, but before he can, the soul hears his reverence by listening alone and asks him why he bends. Dante tells him: because of your dignity, my conscience stung me for standing. The reply is the line this day turns on.
Straighten thy legs, and upward raise thee, brother.
And then: do not make the mistake. He is a fellow-servant, he says, with Dante and with the rest.

A man who held one of the highest offices of his world, flat on his face and bound hand and foot, tells a living stranger to stand up. There is no rank in this place, the poem suggests, and he has learned what it was worth.

What might this mean for a walker? The road is full of things to hold: the gear, the phone, the money, the bed. You need them, and the poem is not against bread or boots or a careful count of what you can afford. It is against being bound. A useful way to tell the difference is to ask whether what you hold is serving the walking or the walking is serving it. And the pope's words are a gift to anyone who has felt small beside someone more experienced, better equipped or simply more confident. The person in the next bunk is a fellow-traveller. So are you.

Three reservations. The picture of lying bound and face down is a stark one, and some readers will find it harsh. We read it as the poem's way of showing the habit, not as a verdict on the people who have it. The second is that counting is not always greed. A walker who budgets carefully is looking after themselves and the people at home. The line lies between counting to live and living to count. The third is that the poet is blunt about rank and about the Church of his own day, and we leave that politics alone. What matters here is a man who learned to say
fellow-servant
The poem's remedy is simple. Look up. Stand. And treat the next person as an equal.
For the walk

items.t: What is my gaze fastened on right now?

Each time you pass a bench, a gate or a bridge, lift your eyes to the farthest thing you can see and hold them there for three breaths. Once today, greet someone as an equal: look at them, say good morning in whatever language you have, and ask them for nothing. Notice how you stand while you do it.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Evening is when we count. The kilometres, the cost of the day, the number of days still to come, the weight of what is left in the pack. It is natural, and it can be useful. So do the counting, and then put it down. Let the figures be what they are for ten minutes, and then close the book.

What held your eyes today? Think back through the hours and look for the places where your head went down for something that was not the path. A screen, a worry about the money, a plan for the next stage, a quiet replay of something you said. None of them was a crime. But ask what you missed while you were looking. There may have been a view, or a face, or a bird on a wall. You cannot get it back, but you can know that it was there.

The pope said that all other burdens seemed a feather beside the cloak. It is worth asking what your cloak is. For some people it is a job, for some a family role, or a reputation, or a sense of being the one who sorts everything out. A road is a place where you can put it down for a while. Nobody here knows your title, and most of what you do is walk. Did you notice the lightness today? If not, it may be because you were still carrying the cloak out of habit.

Think about rank in the smaller sense. Where did you treat someone as above you or below you today? Perhaps a person who seemed to know more, or a host, or a stranger who was not very well dressed. The question is not whether you were rude. It is whether, for a moment, you forgot that you were fellow-travellers. If you remembered, what changed?

The ground is under you tonight, too, and it is holding you up. Lie on a bed or a mat, and you can feel your weight go down through you into something that does not move. It is the same ground the souls cling to in the poem, and tonight it is a friend.

You are going to lie down tonight, and it is worth noticing that it is not the lying down of the poem. Their rest is a restraint. Yours is a choice, and an earned one. It is a gift to be able to lie down on purpose, to a clean sheet, and to know you can stand up in the morning.

One last thing. Give something away tomorrow, however small: a spare plaster, a piece of fruit, a few minutes of attention. It need not be noticed, and it need not be thanked. Open hands are hard to bind.

items.t: What held my gaze today, and what did I miss while it did?
Where did I treat someone as above or below me, and what changed when I did not?
What is one small thing I could give away tomorrow?

spans.t: A short prayer
Lift my eyes from what I hold to what is far off. Loosen my hands and my feet. Let me count what I need and no more. Teach me to stand up. Let me call everyone I meet a fellow traveller.
How do you honour hunger without being ruled by it?
The passage

paras.t: In the same way that thoughtful pilgrims do, Who, unknown people on the road o’ertaking, Turn themselves round to them, and do not stop, Even thus, behind us with a swifter motion Coming and passing onward, gazed upon us A crowd of spirits silent and devout. … Desire to eat and drink enkindles in us The scent that issues from the apple-tree, And from the spray that sprinkles o’er the verdure; And not a single time alone, this ground Encompassing, is refreshed our pain,— I say our pain, and ought to say our solace,— For the same wish doth lead us to the tree Which led the Christ rejoicing to say ‘Eli,’ When with his veins he liberated us. … And heard it said: “Blessed are they whom grace So much illumines, that the love of taste Excites not in their breasts too great desire, Hungering at all times so far as is just.”

cite.t: ), Cantos XXIII and XXIV (tr. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow)

spans.t: Reflection

You pass a kitchen door at the end of a long stage, and the smell reaches you before you have understood where you are. Something frying, bread, onions, the warmth of a place where people cook. You did not know how hungry you were until the smell told you, and now it is the only thing in the street. That is where the sixth ledge of the mountain begins.

The first lines of our passage are not about food at all. They are about the road. A crowd of spirits comes up behind Dante, Virgil and a third traveller, the poet Statius, who has joined them along the way. They are going faster, and the poet compares the way they gaze at the travellers to what thoughtful pilgrims do when they overtake strangers on the road: they turn round to look and do not stop. A glance, perhaps a word, and on. A walker will know the custom.

But these are no ordinary walkers. The crowd is silent and devout, and so wasted that the skin seems to take its shape from the bones. Dante cannot understand what has done it. Then he is told, and it is astonishing: the smell of an apple, and of water. There is a tree on the ledge with fruit and fresh leaves, and a spray of clear water falling over it, and every time the souls pass it their hunger and thirst are kindled again, and they walk on.
One of them looks at Dante from the hollow of his head and cries out,
What grace to me is this?

Dante does not know him by his face, which is altered past knowing. He knows him by his voice. It is Forese, an old friend, whose death Dante once wept over. He begs Dante not to look at his dry, discoloured skin but to say what he is doing here. And Dante answers that the face he mourned when it was dead gives him no less grief to see now, so changed.

Forese explains. The scent of the tree and of the spray kindles in them the desire to eat and drink, and they are making amends for following appetite beyond measure. And then the lines of our passage, the part that matters most:
And not a single time alone, this ground Encompassing, is refreshed our pain,— I say our pain, and ought to say our solace.
The hunger hurts, and it is also, he says, a comfort. He ties it to the cross in the lines that follow, and we leave that to those who share the poet's faith.

He also tells Dante how he got so far up so fast. It was his widow, Nella, whose prayers and tears carried him up from the lower slopes. She is, he says, all the more dear to God for being alone in her good works. You do not have to share the poem's belief in how this works to see what it says about the people at home. Somebody may be holding a thread.

The last lines of the passage come a canto later, after the three travellers have passed another tree. An angel stands in the road, so bright that Dante has to turn away, and tells them to go this way for peace. A breeze touches Dante's forehead, with a scent of something like ambrosia, and a voice says:
Blessed are they whom grace So much illumines, that the love of taste Excites not in their breasts too great desire, Hungering at all times so far as is just.
The last phrase carries it. The blessed are not people who have stopped being hungry. They hunger
at all times
, and what they have learned is to hunger
so far as is just

, which in the poem means: to the right degree. The fault was never the appetite. It was the measure. The poem's idea of the good life is not a body that wants nothing. It is a body whose wanting has the right size.

For a walker, that is practical sense. A long day makes you honestly hungry, and the walking body needs real food and real water, and a good deal of both. Nothing here asks you to go without. What it asks about is the manner: whether you can eat at the end of a day with attention, enjoy the taste, and know when it is enough. The same goes for the second glass.

Two honest cautions. The picture of the wasted faces is stark, and if food is a hard subject for you, if you have had to fight to eat or you feel guilty when you do, take none of it as an instruction. Eat what the day needs. The line to keep is the last one, about the right measure. And you do not have to accept the poem's account of what prayers do. Someone at home thinking of you is a real kind of help, whatever one believes about the rest.
So: eat when you are hungry, slowly, and give thanks to whoever made it. And when you meet someone on the road, do as the pilgrims do in the poem: look, greet, and walk on.
For the walk

items.t: What does my body need right now, and what does my tongue only want?

At your next meal or snack, put the phone away. Eat the first three mouthfuls slowly, and name the taste to yourself. Then eat what you need, and notice the moment when it is enough. If you pass someone on the road, turn and give them a greeting before you walk on.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Supper is the biggest meal of the day for most walkers, and the hunger that comes to meet it is honest. It is nothing to be ashamed of, and it deserves a real meal. If you can, eat it sitting down, away from a screen, and let it take a little time. The first mouthfuls of a meal after a long day are among the best of the whole road. Most of that is missed if you rush.

The poem is wise about the other side of it too. A second helping, a third glass, the dessert you did not want but ordered, are all small matters. They only deserve a thought if they leave you heavy, or if you ate against the grain of what you wanted. Be gentle about it. A day of hard walking is a poor judge of its own appetite, and tomorrow's will be easier to guess.

Think of Forese's phrase, which puts pain and solace in one breath. Was there a discomfort today that turned out, afterwards, to carry something? A thirst that made the water taste of something, a tiredness that made a bench feel like a gift. Not everything works that way, and you do not have to force it. But the best moments of a walking day are very often built out of a need.

But there are other hungers in a day, and the poem hints at them. Which of yours went unfed? There is the hunger for rest, and the hunger for company, and the hunger for a quiet half hour in which nobody wants anything from you. There is the hunger for a view you did not stop for, and the hunger to be asked how you are. Name the one that was loudest today. You may not be able to feed it tonight, but you can say what it is, and sometimes that is half the meal. If it is rest, the bed is already waiting.
Think too of the road. The poet makes a picture of pilgrims passing strangers: a glance, a turn of the head, and they do not stop. Whom did you pass today, or who passed you? A nod, a greeting, a
Buen Camino
said and answered. They may be gone by morning, and the exchange will be what is left. It is a small, steady kindness, and a road is held together by it.

Dante knew Forese by his voice when his face was changed past knowing. Tonight the faces around you are tired and dusty, and your own may not look much like itself. If there is a friend who would know you by your voice, a call or a message would do you good. You do not have to say anything of weight.

items.t: What did my body truly need today, and did I give it?
Which hunger, for food, rest, company or quiet, went unfed today?
Whom did I pass or meet on the road, and did we exchange a word?

spans.t: A short prayer

I am glad of the food, the water and the bed. Teach me the measure of enough, in what I eat and in what I want. Feed the hungers I forgot today, and quiet the ones that shout. Bless the strangers who passed me on the road.

chapters.title: Day 12. The wall and the stair

spans.t: What gets you through the stretch you are afraid of, and what do you do when the light goes?
The passage

paras.t: And I still motionless, and ’gainst my conscience! Seeing me stand still motionless and stubborn, Somewhat disturbed he said: “Now look thou, Son, ’Twixt Beatrice and thee there is this wall.” … When I was in it, into molten glass I would have cast me to refresh myself, So without measure was the burning there! … “The sun departs,” it added, “and night cometh; Tarry ye not, but onward urge your steps, So long as yet the west becomes not dark.” … Each of us of a stair had made his bed; Because the nature of the mount took from us The power of climbing, more than the delight. … And now before the antelucan splendours That unto pilgrims the more grateful rise, As, home-returning, less remote they lodge, The darkness fled away on every side, And slumber with it; whereupon I rose, Seeing already the great Masters risen.

spans.t: Reflection

Most long roads have one stretch that is feared. It is not always the longest or the steepest. It is the one you cannot see round: a steep descent in the wet, a crossing, a road with no verge, or simply the last day, with everything you have put into the walk hanging on it. And then the moment arrives, and it is a few hundred metres of track, and you are in it.

The poem has put a wall of fire across the last stretch of the climb. It lies on the seventh and last ledge, and the day is ending. An angel stands outside the flames and sings. Nobody goes further, he says, unless the fire bites first, so they must go in and listen for the song beyond. Dante hears it and goes pale. He says he became like a man being put into the grave. He clasps his hands, stares into the flames and remembers the bodies of people he has seen burned.
Virgil turns to him, and says the sentence we have all wanted someone to say:
Here may indeed be torment, but not death.

Then he argues. If he has brought Dante safely through the worst of the first part of the journey, what will he do now that he is nearer God? Believe it for certain, he says, you could stand in this fire a thousand years and it would not singe a hair. If you doubt me, go close and hold the hem of your garment to it.
None of this moves Dante. He stands there, in the poem's words, still and stubborn, and
'gainst my conscience
, knowing perfectly well what is true. And at last Virgil, a little troubled, says the thing that works.
Now look thou, Son, 'Twixt Beatrice and thee there is this wall.

That is all. The name is enough. It is like the dying lover in the old story who opens his eyes at the name of the woman he loves. Dante turns to his guide, and Virgil shakes his head and smiles, as one does at a child who has been vanquished by an apple. How now, shall we stay on this side?
Then Virgil goes in first. Our passage gives the truth about what follows.
When I was in it, into molten glass I would have cast me to refresh myself, So without measure was the burning there!
The poem does not pretend it was easy. And Virgil keeps talking all the way through, about the eyes he seems already to see, so that Dante has something to follow besides the heat.

That is the first lesson, and it is a small one. Fear is rarely beaten by argument. It is beaten by a name, a reason, a person, by something you love more than you fear. If you find yourself frozen at the edge of a stretch you dread, you may do well to say why you are here. Say who you are walking for. And if you can, go with someone who will go in first.

The second lesson is in the stairs. On the far side a voice sings, and the travellers follow it up a stair cut straight through the rock. The voice also gives a rule: the sun is leaving, and night is coming, so do not linger but go on while the west is not yet dark. They climb a few stairs, and the sun sets behind them. And then comes the sentence that this book keeps coming back to: each of them made a bed of a stair,
Because the nature of the mount took from us The power of climbing, more than the delight.

Read it slowly. It is not that they no longer want to climb. The delight is intact. What the mountain withdraws is the power, at night, and it does so as a law of its nature. Nobody is blamed. Dante lies down, sees the stars larger and brighter than he has known them, and sleeps. The poem insists that a night is part of the climb.

On a real road the point has a practical edge. Dusk on an unfamiliar path is when walking is most dangerous. Plan to be indoors before the light goes. If you cannot, ask for a lift or a bed, and stop early. No one will think less of you.
And look at how the night ends.
And now before the antelucan splendours That unto pilgrims the more grateful rise, As, home-returning, less remote they lodge.
The light before dawn is more welcome to pilgrims, the poem says, the nearer they lodge to home. The last mornings are the sweetest.

Two points of honesty. The Camino has no wall of fire, and the poem's sentence is not that it will not hurt. It is that it will hurt and will not kill. If your fear is about a real danger, a river in flood or a bad fall, listen to it, because it may be right. The sentence is for the fear that is mostly about the unknown. And the last ledge, the poem's ledge of love that ran too hot, is not one this book follows.
For the walk

items.t: Which wall am I afraid of today, and what name would get me through it?

When you meet a stretch that frightens you, say once, aloud or silently, the name of the person or the reason you are walking for. Then take the first step, and do not stop to argue. Before you set out, find out when the light goes today, and decide where you will be indoors by then.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Tonight you are doing what the three travellers did at the top of their stairs. You have come to where you cannot, or will not, climb any further, and you are lying down where the day has put you. It is the right thing to do. The mountain thought so.

Was there a wall today? It need not have been a big one. A stretch you disliked the look of, a conversation you had been putting off, a hill that seemed to go on being a hill. Think about how you met it. Did you walk straight at it, or around the edge of it for an hour? Did anything carry you in? And what was it like on the other side? The poem does not linger there. Dante barely mentions the fire once it is behind him. A frightening thing, once crossed, tends to shrink to a few lines.

Then the name. Whose, or what, would you have said at the wall? You may not need it tonight, but tomorrow or the day after you will meet another stretch, and it helps to have the answer ready. If you do not know, that is a fair thing to have found out. A reason is worth looking for, and it will keep.

If you can see the sky from where you are, look at it. Dante saw the stars on the stairs larger than he had known them, and the sight is part of what he took to bed. You do not need to name anything. A few minutes of looking up will do more for you than another look at the phone.

And think about the power and the delight. There may have been a moment today when you wanted to go on and could not, or when you went on and perhaps should not have. The mountain's law is honest about it. Wanting is not enough, and the body's no is not an insult. You can keep the desire and give the night its due. Tomorrow's strength is being made while you lie here, which is something the lying down is for.

Before you sleep, make ready for the dawn. Boots by the door, water filled, the first hour in your mind. The poem says that the light before sunrise is the more welcome the nearer pilgrims lodge to home, and it helps to give it something to be welcome to: a clean sock, a clear head, a plan that is only the first few kilometres.
If you ever cannot be indoors by dusk, tell somebody, a host, a companion, a friend on the phone, where you are and where you mean to sleep. The mountain's law is easier to keep with a witness.
You may be tired enough now that none of this matters. That is as it should be. Eat, drink and sleep, and let the dawn come to you.

items.t: Which wall did I meet today, and what carried me through it?
Whose name, or what reason, would I say if I were afraid tomorrow?
Where did I stop today because the day asked me to, and did I let that be enough?

spans.t: A short prayer
Be with me at the wall, and go in before me. Give me a name to say when I am afraid. Let this night be a stair I can lie down on. Let the dawn be kind. Keep the ones I love while I sleep.
What if the guide has done his part, and tells you to lead?
The passage

paras.t: And said: “The temporal fire and the eternal, Son, thou hast seen, and to a place art come Where of myself no farther I discern. By intellect and art I here have brought thee; Take thine own pleasure for thy guide henceforth; Beyond the steep ways and the narrow art thou. Behold the sun, that shines upon thy forehead; Behold the grass, the flowerets, and the shrubs Which of itself alone this land produces. Until rejoicing come the beauteous eyes Which weeping caused me to come unto thee, Thou canst sit down, and thou canst walk among them. Expect no more or word or sign from me; Free and upright and sound is thy free-will, And error were it not to do its bidding; Thee o’er thyself I therefore crown and mitre!” … Eager already to search in and round The heavenly forest, dense and living-green, Which tempered to the eyes the new-born day, Withouten more delay I left the bank, Taking the level country slowly, slowly Over the soil that everywhere breathes fragrance.

cite.t: ), Cantos XXVII and XXVIII (tr. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow)

spans.t: Reflection

At some point on a long walk you notice that you have stopped checking. You know what a waymark looks like, you can read the lie of the land, and you trust your feet to find the line of the path. The guidebook is in the pack, the arrows are friendly, and you simply walk. It happens gradually, and then there is a day when you notice that it has happened.

Dante's guide has been with him since the first canto of the poem. At the top of the stairs, with the last fire behind them, Virgil turns and fixes his eyes on him, and makes a speech. It is the farewell speech of a teacher, and the strange thing is how brief and how plain it is.
The temporal fire and the eternal
, he says, Dante has seen, the fire that ends and the fire that does not, and he has come to a place where Virgil himself can see no further.
By intellect and art I here have brought thee.
That is what Virgil is in the poem: human reason and human craft, and a good deal of both, which have carried a man this far and cannot carry him any further.
Then comes the line that startles:
Take thine own pleasure for thy guide henceforth.

Dante is beyond the steep and narrow ways, Virgil says. Let him look at the sun on his forehead, and at the grass, the flowers and the shrubs that this ground grows by itself. Until the beautiful eyes arrive, the eyes whose weeping sent Virgil to him in the first place, he may sit down, and he may walk among them. Those eyes belong to the lady from heaven who sent Virgil, and readers of the poem have long taken her to be Beatrice.
Expect no more or word or sign from me.
Dante's will, says Virgil, is free, upright and sound, and it would be an error not to follow it. And then the last line, the one that gives the day its title:
Thee o'er thyself I therefore crown and mitre!
A crown is a king's and a mitre is a bishop's. Virgil is saying that Dante has authority over himself.

The second half of the passage is one of the loveliest walks in the poem. Dante, eager to explore, goes alone into the heavenly forest, which is thick and living green and which softens the new day for his eyes. He leaves the bank and takes the level ground
slowly, slowly
, over soil that breathes fragrance everywhere. In the lines that follow, a soft wind bends the branches all one way, and the birds do not stop singing in the treetops. Nobody tells him where to go.
Three things in this deserve a moment. The first is the guide's limit. Virgil does not pretend.
Where of myself no farther I discern.
A good guide knows where their sight ends, and says so. What the guide leaves you is yourself. The most generous thing a guidebook, a friend or a teacher can do is to become unnecessary.

The second is the line about pleasure, which is easy to misread. It does not mean doing whatever you like, and it should not be taken as a licence on the first day of a walk. On the poem's terms, Dante's wants have been trained by the whole climb, and the question of what he wants and what is good have drawn together. The line describes where the climb arrives, not where it starts. On a long road you may find, by the second or third week, that what you want, a bench, a coffee, a silence, a hill, and what is good for you lie closer to one another than they did at the beginning. That is only a possibility, and nothing here depends on it.
The third is the
slowly, slowly

. After the stairs, the level ground. The poem could have hurried through it, and instead it repeats the word. On a road, the easy stretch is where the temptation is to speed up because you can. The poem suggests the reverse: the flat, kind country is the one to take slowly.

There is a loss in it too. Virgil is still beside Dante when this canto ends, listening with a smile, but he no longer steers. A little later, in Canto XXX, Dante turns to him as a child runs to its mother, and finds he is gone:
Virgilius, sweetest of all fathers
. The poem lets that be as abrupt as such partings are. It is worth knowing that the freedom here has a price, and that some of it is silence.
If you have had a guide on this road, of any kind, you may find today that you are more alone than you expected, and also that you are fine.
For the walk

items.t: Where could I trust myself today without checking?

Choose one small decision, which side of the street, where to rest, what pace, and make it from what you want, without asking anyone or looking anything up. Then, when the way is level and kind, slow down. Walk a hundred steps
slowly, slowly
, and see what the ground and the air have to say.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Begin with thanks. Who or what has guided you on this road? A book, a friend, a stranger, a waymark, the voice in your head that says
left here

. The yellow arrow is a particular kind of guide: it never explains, and it never tires, and it only points. You may never have thanked any of them. Do it now, in your mind, one by one. It takes a minute, and it is a way of closing the account. If one of them is a person, a single sentence to them tomorrow will do.

Then think about where you decided things yourself today. It need not be anything grand. Where to stop, whether to take the longer way round, whether to talk or to be quiet. Look at how it felt. Was it easy and clear, or did you want someone to tell you? And how did it turn out? If it was good, notice that. If it was not, notice that too, without scolding. The poem trusts a will that has been through something, and you have been through some days.
The poem has Virgil say that Dante could sit down or walk. Notice which you did today. Both are the same freedom, and neither is more virtuous.

Silence is the other thing Virgil gives, and it is not the same for everyone. A day with no voice to tell you what to do might have felt lonely, or it might have felt like air. Either is a fair report. If it was lonely, the poem does not call that a fault. A road has its lonely stretches, and the freedom to be alone comes with them.

And the slow part: was there a level stretch today, and did you take it slowly? If you hurried, there may be another one tomorrow. The flat road is a gift that does not come as often as one would like.

Try a small experiment before you sleep. Ask yourself what you want, right now, this minute, and answer honestly: a glass of water, a hot shower, silence, a voice on the phone. Do it, if you can. It is a very small crowning, and the poem's trust in a trained will can only be tested in small things like this.

A last, quiet thought. The road is coming to its end, or the book is, or both. Some of the people you have met will go another way soon. It is early to say goodbye, and there is no need to do it tonight. But it is not too early to keep a little attention for them. Notice one person today whose company you would not like to lose, and tell them so, if it feels right, in a sentence.

items.t: Where did I decide something today from my own wanting, and how did it turn out?
Who or what has been my guide on this road, and have I thanked them?
Where could I have gone more slowly, and what might I have seen?

spans.t: A short prayer

For every guide I have had, the loud ones and the silent ones, I am grateful. When the words stop, teach me to trust what the road has taught me. Let my wanting be honest and my steps slow, and let me sleep.

chapters.title: Day 14. New leaves on an old tree

spans.t: What will you leave at the first river, what will you take from the second, and what will you carry home?
The passage

paras.t: In front of them the Tigris and Euphrates Methought I saw forth issue from one fountain, And slowly part, like friends, from one another. … I will too, if not written, at least painted, Thou bear it back within thee, for the reason That cinct with palm the pilgrim’s staff is borne. … If, Reader, I possessed a longer space For writing it, I yet would sing in part Of the sweet draught that ne’er would satiate me; But inasmuch as full are all the leaves Made ready for this second canticle, The curb of art no farther lets me go. From the most holy water I returned Regenerate, in the manner of new trees That are renewed with a new foliage, Pure and disposed to mount unto the stars.

spans.t: Reflection

Roads end in ordinary places. If yours finishes in Santiago de Compostela, as the Norte does, you will arrive in a city where ordinary life is going on around you, and you will be a little dusty and a great deal tired, with a whole road's worth of feeling and nowhere particular to put it. If you are reading at home, the equivalent is closing a book. Either way, the question of the last day is the same. What goes with you, and what stays?
The poem's last canto answers in pictures. Dante and Beatrice and the others come to a shady place at the edge of the garden, where two streams rise from a single spring and
slowly part, like friends, from one another

. He has been told about these waters already. One, called Lethe, takes away all memory of wrongdoing. The other, called Eunoe, gives back the memory of every good deed done. He has already drunk from the first. Now Beatrice tells the lady of the garden to lead him to the second and revive what is half-dead in him.

Hold that picture of the rivers. One source, two directions. A thing that parts slowly, like friends. It may be the best image in the poem for the last day of a pilgrimage, because it is true of the people you have walked with. You came along the same stretch for a while, and now you will go different ways, and nobody has to be wrenched apart. The poem's friends part slowly. You can let yours.

Then Beatrice does something unexpected. She has been speaking in riddles for a good while, and she tells Dante to take what he has heard back with him. If it cannot be written, she says, then at least painted:
I will too, if not written, at least painted, Thou bear it back within thee, for the reason That cinct with palm the pilgrim's staff is borne.

The pilgrim who comes home brings his staff wound round with palm, as a sign of where he has been. The Way has its own token, the scallop shell, which many people wear or carry on a pack. The poem's point is wider than a keepsake. She does not ask for an essay. A picture will do, one image that holds the whole, brought back inside you.

After that, the poet does something rarer. He stops. If he had more space for writing, he says, he would sing a little of the sweet draught that never leaves him satisfied. But the leaves made ready for this canticle are full, and
The curb of art no farther lets me go.

He stops because he has run out of pages, not because he has run out of things to say. A road ends the same way, at the measure it was given and not at the point where wanting stops. You may find that you want to go on, and that is the sign of a good road, and not a failure of the walking.
And then the final sentence:
From the most holy water I returned Regenerate, in the manner of new trees That are renewed with a new foliage, Pure and disposed to mount unto the stars.

Take it a word at a time. He returned, like a tree. A tree is not a new tree each spring. It is the same one with new leaves. That may be the most truthful thing in the poem for a person coming home. You are not replaced. You are renewed, and a good deal of what is old in you is still standing. And he is
disposed
to mount, which is a long way short of having arrived. The poem ends with a readiness, not an arrival. And the word it ends on is
stars
, the same sky that was over the shore on the first morning, when four of them stood over the old man at the water's edge.
Three things to be straight about. The first is that nobody finishes a road
pure

. A walker comes in with blisters and mixed feelings, and some of what was heavy on Day 1 is still heavy on Day 14. The poem's claim is the poem's own. You are allowed to read it as a wish, and a good one. The second is that the two rivers do not ask you to forget everything. The first washes away what is bad, and the second keeps what is good. If the good fades first, as it can, the second river is the one to look for. And the third is that the last day may be flat. Nobody has said it will arrive like the sapphire dawn of the first morning, and if it does not, nothing has gone wrong.
So the day has three small tasks, all of them light. Choose one thing to put in the first river. Choose one good thing to take from the second. And choose one picture to carry home.
For the walk

items.t: What will I leave at the first river, what will I take from the second, and what picture will I carry home?

On the last stretch of your walk, or the last quiet minutes of your reading, choose three things: one thing to forget, such as a grudge, a blister or a worry; one good thing to remember; and one image of the road. Say each once, in a sentence, aloud if nobody is near. Then simply walk.

spans.t: At the end of the day

This is the last evening of the book, and it may or may not be the last evening of your road. If you are still walking, the poem would not mind your reading this tomorrow, or in a week. If you are at the end, it is the right night to be a little quiet.

Start with the rivers. Is there something you would like to put in the first one? It does not have to be heavy, and if the road is not yet over, none of this is urgent. The rivers will wait. It may be a small resentment about a bed, or the memory of a day that went wrong, or the picture of yourself at the bottom of a hill. Say what it is, and let the water take it. The poem does not ask for much. It only asks you to be willing.

And the second. Of everything that happened, what do you want to keep? The poem's drink is one that restores the memory of the good that was done, whoever did it. Some of it was yours, and some was other people's: the stranger with the directions, the person who held a door, the host who left a light on. Make a little list, in your head or on paper. These are what you will tell people about, and they are easily lost if you do not collect them tonight.

Then the people. Who have you walked beside, and how will you part? The poem's rivers go slowly, like friends. If there is someone whose company you would like to keep, there may be a way to say so before you go your own ways. If there is someone you simply liked, a word of thanks is a good thing to leave. Parting does not have to be a wound.

Look at your feet before you sleep. They did this. They carried you the whole way, and some of it was hard on them. A sentence of thanks is not silly: some of the honest things to say tonight are to a body, and it has been listening all along.

And be honest about how you feel. The end of a road, or a book, often brings something other than joy: flatness, a kind of grief, restlessness, sometimes nothing at all. All of those are ordinary. The poem's last line is a readiness, not a fanfare. You have done what you have done, and tomorrow will start without any ceremony.
If you can, go out for a minute and look at the sky. The poem ends on its stars. It is a good place to put your attention, and a good place to lay it down.

items.t: What do I want to leave at the first river, and what do I want to keep from the second?
Who have I walked beside, and how can I part from them like a friend?
What one picture of this road would I carry home, even if I could not write it down?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the road, the people and the days, thank you. Take from me what I should forget, and keep for me what was good. Let me go home as the same tree with new leaves. Let me carry one picture. Turn my face to the stars, and let me rest.

You have come to the end of the fourteen days, or you have stopped early, or you mean to go on slowly. All three are fine. This book gives out no certificate. It was meant as company on a road, and a road has no use for a book once the road is done, except to be remembered kindly.
So only one question is left, which is what to take down the mountain with you.
Not everything. Nobody carries a whole poem. Choose three small things.

items.t: A line.
Something Dante said that stayed in your head. It might be
And aye the more one climbs, the less it hurts.
It might be
Hearing shall keep us joined instead thereof
, or
Hungering at all times so far as is just
, or just two words,
slowly, slowly
. Write it on a card, or on the inside of something you will see every morning.
A ledge.

The mountain has seven, and each is a weight: pride, envy, anger, sloth, greed, appetite, and, at the top, a love that ran too hot, which this book only passed through. You may recognise one of them as yours. The poem does not ask you to be finished with it. It asks you to know which one you carry, and to notice when it is heavy.
A name.
The one you would say at the wall of fire. A person, or a reason, or a place. Keep it where you can reach it, because the stretch you are afraid of tends to turn up when you are tired.

spans.t: If you can keep all three for a month, you will have kept more than most people keep from any book.
How to go on

Go back whenever you like. The days are short and were made to be read more than once. A day that did nothing for you at the shore may say a great deal on a hard hill later on. Read the evenings alone for a week. Read a single passage aloud on a bad morning and nothing else. Or read the days in the order the weather gives you, not the order of the poem.
You might also read Dante himself. This book has used a small part of one third of a long poem, and every word of it, in this translation, is in the public domain. The
Purgatorio
is in the same translation, from Project Gutenberg, ebook number 1002. The whole poem, with the
Inferno

And be honest about what did not work. Some days will have rubbed. Some passages will have been strange or hard, or asked for more than you could give. That is allowed. A book of this kind is not a test. If a day did not speak to you, nothing has gone wrong. Leave it, and take what did.
A last word

Dante wrote this poem far from home, in the years when he could not go back. He ends it with no triumph. He says the pages are full, and that he came back from the water renewed, like trees with new leaves, ready to rise. Not arrived. Ready.

That may be all that a road can honestly give. You do not have to know where the next stretch leads. You need a next step, some patience with yourself, a name to say when you are afraid, and now and then a hand on the shoulder at the right moment.
Walk again. Next year, if you can. Or tomorrow, round the block, with your phone in your pocket and your hands open.
Buen Camino.
